LECTURE 1.3: A High-Level Overview of Web Development
----------------------------------------

Instructor: Welcome to the first actual lecture of this course. Now, there is a good chance that this course is gonna be your very first contact with any web development. And so before we start writing HTML and CSS code, I think it might be a good idea to actually begin this course with a very high-level overview of this field of web development. So we're gonna talk about things like clients and servers, front-end and back-end development, static and dynamic websites, and of course about the core languages and core technologies of web development.

And I'm going to explain all this around the process that happens when we open up a webpage in a browser. Just keep in mind again that this is just a high-level overview and so I'm gonna leave out a lot of details here. This is really just so you get familiar with some of these concepts and terms that all web developers know before you start your own journey. But anyway, let's say that we're trying to access a webpage in our browser at omnifood.dev.

And by the way, this is actually the website that we're gonna develop throughout this course. Now, what happens as we try to access this page is that our browser will send a request to the server where this page is hosted on the internet. So each and every website is stored on something called a server, which is basically a computer that is connected to the internet and is able to receive requests like this one. So again, when we browse to a certain website our web browser will send a request to the server where the website is stored, so where it is hosted.

Then when the server receives the request, it will take all the files that make up the website and send them back to the browser. And so we say that the server sends a response to the browser, which essentially contains all of these files that the website is made of. Now, as you can see from these file extensions we have some HTML, CSS, and also JavaScript code here. And these are precisely the three languages that browsers can understand. So what this means is that all of the code that makes up a website needs to always be written in HTML, CSS, and JavaScript because again, these are essentially the three core technologies that any browser can understand.

All right, now, once the browser receives these HTML, CSS, and JavaScript files from the service response, it will take the code and render the website that we were trying to access. So based on that code, okay? And with this you already have a good understanding of what actually happens when we browse to a website and also about the technologies that we use to build any website. And that process of writing HTML, CSS and JavaScript code that the browser can understand is the process that we call front-end web development.

So whenever you hear someone talking about front-end development, what they mean is developers writing the code that is displayed in a browser, which is basically the front-end of a website. And in fact, this is essentially what we're gonna learn in this course, or at least the very, very fundamentals of front-end development, which is learning HTML and CSS. Now, just as a side note here, whenever the files that make up the website are simply stored on the web server and are then sent to the browser as they are, we say that we have a static website, okay?

And this will make a little bit more sense in a minute when we talk about what a dynamic website is. But for now, just keep in mind that a static website is basically a website where the files are simply sent from the server to the browser as they are, so without any transformations, all right? So I hope that from this you learned what front-end development is, and also about the three core technologies that make up any website. And so now let's take it one step further and talk about something called back-end development.

So let's try another example here, and this time let's try to understand what would happen when we try to access a website like udemy.com. So once again, the first step is that a request is sent to the web server where udemy.com is hosted. Now, why is a website like udemy so different from something like the static omnifood website that I showed you earlier? Well, a complex site like udemy.com is really completely different from a static site because there is a lot of content that is always changing all the time.

Like on Udemy, there are always new courses and new reviews being added to the site. New ratings, and new course length are calculated for example, and really a bunch of other things like that are always happening. And so in order to make a system like this work udemy.com needs a whole application running on the server and they also need a big database, which basically contains all the courses, and all the reviews, all the users, and really all the content that is being displayed on their website.

Now, to do all this front-end technologies like HTML and CSS are simply not enough. So basically, with what you're gonna learn in this course, you are not going to be able to build something like udemy.com, all right? So to write applications that are actually executed on web servers, developers use some kind of back-end language like Node.js, PHP, or Python. So what these languages do is to take data out of a database and basically assemble that data into the final files that will then be sent to the browser as the response.

And this whole process is called back-end development because this is basically the invisible part of a website and so it's the website's back-end. Now, in this situation, we say that we have a dynamic website because the website is dynamically assembled from different pieces on the server and that happens each time that someone visits the website. So returning to the example of udemy.com, in fact each time that you visit udemy, a new version of the website is gonna be generated from their database and sent to your browser.

Now, on the other hand, if udemy was a static website, then the website files would already be sitting on the server just waiting for someone to access them, okay? So that's the big difference between static and dynamic. In static, the files are already done and in dynamic, they first need to be generated by an application that is running on the server. All right, but now the rest of the process is actually the same as before. So these files are now ready to be sent to the browser as a response, which will then be converted to the final website like this one we see here of udemy.com.

Great. Now, of course, there is no need for you to memorize all these names that I mentioned here, and also no need to deeply understand this process. All I want here is to give you an overview of what front-end and back-end actually are, what the browser and the server are, and also what static and dynamic websites are. Because I really think that this is gonna be extremely helpful as you start your developer journey. But now just to finish, let's take a closer look at the three languages of the front-end, so HTML, CSS, and JavaScript.

And starting with HTML, HTML is responsible for the content of the page. So that's the text, the images, the buttons, and really all the content that you see on a webpage is always written inside an HTML file. Then the CSS, is responsible for the presentation of that content, so basically for styling and for laying out the elements on the webpage. Now finally, JavaScript is the actual programming language of the front-end. So it allows us to add dynamic and interactive effects to webpages.

We can also use it to manipulate the content or the CSS to load data from web servers and even to build entire front-end applications, which we then call web applications. Now, we can also use the analogy of nouns, adjectives, and verbs to make the separation of rolls here a little bit easier to understand. So in this analogy, HTML represents the nouns, for example, saying that the p element is a paragraph. So paragraph is the noun here. The CSS then is the adjective because it basically describes the noun, for example, like this piece of CSS saying that the paragraph text is red.

And so red is the adjective describing the noun, all right? Finally, JavaScript is of course the verb, like saying, hide the paragraph. So we're actually doing something here and so we have a verb, okay? Does that make sense? All right, and with this we finish our introduction to web development, and so we're now ready to start working with HTML and CSS code in this course.

LECTURE 2.2: Introduction to HTML
----------------------------------------

Instructor: Welcome back. Let's now very quickly learn what HTML actually is and what we can do with it. So basically, HTML stands for hypertext markup language. And remember how we learned earlier that HTML is one of the core web technologies, along with CSS and JavaScript, right? Now, HTML is a markup language that we web developers can use to structure and describe the entire content of any webpage. So notice how I said markup language because HTML is really not a programming language.

It's a markup language because we use it to describe something. And in the case of HTML, we do describe content using elements. So we have different elements that we can use to describe different types of content. So, for example, we have the <p> element that we already used in the lecture where we created our very first webpage. And so we used the <p> element there to create a paragraph, but we really have all kinds of different elements. So elements to create links, to create page headings, images, video, and a lot more, as you'll learn throughout this section and basically throughout the entire course.

Then as we also learned in that lecture where we built our very first webpage, web browsers, such as Google Chrome, do essentially understand HTML code and can render it as a final website, so a website that we can see in the browser. Okay, so this is essentially what HTML is and what we can do with it. But now, let's just zoom in a little bit and take a look at the anatomy of an HTML element. So basically, take a look at the building blocks of each HTML element.

And again, we are looking at the paragraph element here, as you can see by the <p>. And so all of this here is actually the element itself. Now, an HTML element is usually made up of three parts. First is the opening tag, which is the name of the element. So, in this case, it's the <p> wrapped in the less than and the greater than symbols. Probably, they have some other names, but that's how I like to call the symbols. So it's less than <p> and then greater than.

Then after that, we have basically the content of the element. So in this example, that is just text, but there might be other types of content. For example, an element can contain in itself another element, which we then call a child element. Also, some elements, such as images, have actually no content at all and have only an opening tag. And all of this will, of course, become very intuitive as we start writing HTML. This is just so that you know what I'm talking about when I speak of opening tag or closing tag, or content.

And speaking of the closing tag, it is basically the same as the opening tag, but with a slash. So we open this paragraph element simply with the <p>. And we then close it with </p>. Okay? Now, for elements that do not have content, such as the image element that I mentioned before, we actually omit the closing tag. So, in that case, we only have the opening tag, and that's it. And we will see that in action, of course, once we start integrating images into a webpage.

Okay, and that's really all you need in order to start learning HTML and practice, which is exactly what we will do in the next lecture.

That the img element is a special element, and that's because it doesn't have any content, and therefore it also doesn't have a closing tack. Now you might wonder if we don't specify any content here for this image element, then how will HTML know which element it should display? LECTURE 2.9: A Note on Semantic HTML
----------------------------------------

Instructor: So I mentioned the term semantic HTML a couple of times in this section and so let's now actually very quickly define what I actually mean by semantic HTML. So in HTML, when we talk about semantics, what we mean is that certain elements have actually a meaning or a purpose attached to them. So when we think about a certain HTML element, we should actually not think about what that element looks like as it's rendered on the page but instead, we should think about what that element actually means and what it stands for.

So that is basically the definition of semantic HTML. Now, not all elements in HTML are semantic. And actually, I talked a little bit about that before here in this element. So the strong element, which makes our element look bold here on the page. So remember how previously I used the b element, which simply turns its content bold but doesn't attach it any meaning, right? So I explained that before and so now maybe it makes a bit more sense. So again, by using the strong element here, the text will still look bold here in the browser but what really matters here is that we now assign some meaning to this content here.

We now say that it's a strong content, which means basically a very important piece of content. And the same here for this piece. So this fundamental word here. So again, we use em for emphasizing this. And so it still looks italic here on the webpage but what we really mean is that we emphasized this word here. So we gave it a special emphasis and yeah, that's what this element here right now means. Okay? And the same is actually true for all of these elements that we used in the last video.

So for example here, this navigation element. All this does is to create a box, remember, which then contains these four anchor elements but visually, it doesn't really do anything. All this does is to represent as a meaning that this is a navigation. But instead of using nav, we could have also used a more generic element, which is the div element. So for example, div. Open and close it here. And again, visually, nothing will change. And so all this did was to create a new box but a box without any meaning.

So that's what div stands for. So back in the day before HTML5, we always used divs for every single box that we needed like this on the page. But then HTML5 came around and introduced this concept of semantic HTML. And so now we should only use the div element when we don't want to attach a certain meaning to a certain container. So to a certain like box element on our page. So in this case, we really want this to mean that it's a navigation and so we use the navigation element for that.

Okay? And the same is true for the article, the header, the footer that we have down here. And in fact, it is true even for the paragraph, for example, because all that this paragraph here and all the other paragraphs really are are essentially boxes filled with text. Now, the p, of course, does have a semantic meaning. It means that it is a paragraph. But we could again use a generic box without any meaning, so this div, and nothing would change visually.

Okay? Actually something did change here. So we lost some of the white space that we do have around the p. All right? So let's put it back here anyway to the p because we want it to have some meaning. And of course, we also want the spacing that the browser gives us by default around the p elements. Okay? But the idea that I mentioned still holds because we could very easily recreate this space here using some CSS later. So if we wanted, we could, in fact, build the entire webpage only out of div elements if we wanted, and then use CSS to style them as we want.

But, of course, we don't do that. We use semantic HTML to give our elements meaning. Now, you might ask why we actually do that and there are multiple reasons. And I think I mentioned them already actually. So one of them is search engine optimization, which basically means that search engines, such as Google will be able to understand the structure of your content, and therefore, they will be better able to analyze what your content and what your webpage is all about.

Also, writing semantic HTML is extremely important for accessibility, and especially for people who rely on screen readers to consume our webpages. Okay? So I hope that this makes sense and we will also keep touching on the subject as we go through the rest of the course. But I still wanted to make it very clear from the very beginning that when we think about HTML, we should not only think about how it actually looks like in the browser but even more what these elements actually mean and what they stand for.

And with that being said, we kind of finished all we had to learn in this section. And so in the next video, we will configure VS Code a little bit more and then we will move on to two final challenges in this section. So don't wait and let's move on to the next lecture here.

LECTURE 3.2: Introduction to CSS
----------------------------------------

Lecturer: Welcome to the first lecture about CSS. So just like we did in the HTML fundamental section, in this section, we will also start by looking at what CSS actually is and we will learn some common terminology so that you always know what I'm talking about when I refer to different pieces of the CSS code. So first of all, CSS stands for cascading style sheets, and just like html, CSS is also one of the core technologies of the web. Now remember that we use HTML to basically describe the content of a page.

And on the other hand, we use CSS to describe the visual style and the presentation of the content that we previously wrote using HTML. So CSS and HTML work very closely together. And in fact, down here you can see a webpage which is actually the project that we will build later in the course. So in the left side, you have just the content, so just the HTML. And then on the right side you have the exact same HTML code, but with a lot of CSS. And so that CSS describes the visual style and also the layout basically of that whole content.

Now, as you already know, HTML consists of a bunch of different elements that we can use to describe the content. And so again, CSS is similar to that because CSS consists of countless properties that we developers can then use to format the content. And these properties allow us to format different things about the font, the text, the general spacing, layout of the page, and so on and so forth. There is really lots of different properties, and of course you don't need to know all of them by heart.

There's just no need for that. The way that you learn these properties is that you use the most important ones over and over again and at one point it will then become very intuitive. Okay, so this is what CSS is all about. So let's now take a look at an actual piece of CSS code. So this is what a typical small piece of CSS might look like, and it always starts with a selector. So for example, if we want to style all the H1 elements on the page, we need to select it in CSS and then we can apply some styles to it.

And so each of these styles, we can call it a declaration. So for example, here we set the font size to 20 pixels. And so that font size is called the property. And the 20 pixels is the value that we declare for that font size property. And so property and value together is a declaration and we can also more casually call it a style. Then all of these declarations or styles together make up the declaration block. So we have these curly braces after the selector.

And so inside of the declaration block, go all the different declarations. So all our styles. And all this together, so basically the selector plus the declaration block is what we call a CSS rule. And so what this means is that in the end or CSS code will be a lot of different CSS rules one after another where we select all of our elements and style them in any way that we want. Okay, and so that is exactly what we will start doing in the next video.

So let's go there right now.

So remember there were three ways of writing CSS, and the first one was Inline CSS. So let me start by showing you how Inline CSS works. And Inline CSS is basically just writing the CSS code inside essentially of the element. So let's say that we wanted to style this text here, blue.

So this h1. We could declare the style attribute like this. And then inside of this HTML element and inside of this HTML file, we would then start writing our CSS. And so let's now move on to the second way of writing CSS, which is called Internal CSS. So with Internal CSS, we come here to the head and then we declare a style element. So style. And then we can write our CSS right here into this style element. So basically, this entire page is HTML, but everything that is inside this style element that needs to be inside of the head will be CSS.

And so now let's write something very similar to what we wrote by the end of the last video. And again, that is what we talked about by the end of the last lecture.

And if we now save it and reload, then you see that once again, the code turned blue here. So this entire text just became blue. Great. So this is already a huge step forward because now we decoupled the style, which is all of this year from the actual HTML element. So before, as we had the style here, then the CSS and the HTML were kind of entangled and that is never a good thing in programming.

And so we want to keep these things in separate places. We also call it the separation of concerns. And so now we have our style here, so everything up in the head and the elements down here separated. However, if we have a lot of CSS code, then that is also not really practical. So imagine we have like 500 lines of CSS code and that is actually not uncommon. And so in that case, that would bloat our HTML file and it would be very hard to navigate it.

And so therefore, we can separate things even more by putting all of our CSS code into a special CSS file. So let's do that. So we click here again on new file. And this one here can have any name, but I like to call it style.css. Okay? So in HTML, the first page should usually always be called index.html. That's really a convention. But for the CSS file, you can give it any name that you want, but again, I like to call it style.css. Okay? And so this is what we now call External CSS, because we will move now this declaration block or this rule actually into a completely different file.

And so this CSS is now external to the HTML. Okay? So we have our style here and now we no longer need the style in here. Now maybe you notice that as I saved this, the blue color is actually gone. So why do you think that is happening? So why is this text no longer blue, even though we have the exact same code here as we had before? Well, the reason is that HTML right now has no way of knowing that we actually do have a CSS file, or in other words, the HTML file and the CSS file do not automatically get linked.

So what we need to do is to tell our HTML file that there is a CSS file that we want to use to style the HTML. So we need to link them together basically. And we do that once again here in the HTML head, because that is exactly where all the information about the page goes. And for that, we use the link element. So that's yet another new element. And the link element is actually quite confusing for beginners because many people when they start out, they might think that the link element is actually to create hyperlinks like here, but that is, of course, not the case.

So as you know already, to create hyperlinks, we use the anchor tech, so not the link tech. So the link element really only has the only purpose of connecting the HTML to a CSS file. So here, we specify href once again, and then here, we need the path to the CSS file. And so in that case, this is just style.css. Then here, it is also good to specify the rel property and tell the HTML ahead of time that this is a style sheet. And now when I save this again, watch what happens.

And nice, our text here is blue again. And so now we successfully connected our CSS file right here to our HTML file. So this is now External CSS, and it is what we will use throughout the rest of the course. And it's also what advise you to do for whenever you build your own webpages. However, Internal CSS also sometimes has its place, especially, when you just want to build something small and fast and want to do everything in the same file, then it is perfectly acceptable to create Internal CSS using these style element, remember?

So just like this. But Inline CSS, which is what I showed you in the very beginning. So adding this style right here using the style attribute, that is usually not a good practice. And so it's not a good idea to do that. All right. And with this now in place, we are ready to start learning our very first couple of CSS properties for styling text. And so that is going to be the subject of our next lecture.

LECTURE 3.7: Working With Colors
----------------------------------------

-: Welcome back. In this lecture, we will learn how to work with colors in CSS. However, before we can actually go back to our CSS we first need to learn a little bit about the theory of how to represent colors using code. Now, there are many ways of representing colors in computers and basically in writing code but one of the more traditional models is the RGB model. So in the RGB model, every single color can be represented by any combination of red, green and blue colors.

So that looks something like this and maybe you have already seen a diagram like this somewhere in school or something like that. So anyway, in order to actually represent a certain color we need to give each of the three base colors any value between zero and 255. And so with that, we can define a total of 16.8 million different colors. So let's understand this a little bit using our diagram here and starting with the pure red color. Of course, in this channel, red is at the complete maximum which is 255 and the other two channels.

So the other two base colors are at zero. So there's no green whatsoever and no blue whatsoever. And so this is why this is pure red. So again, the red channel is at the maximum value and all the other ones are at zero and the same of course for blue and for green. So in blue, the blue channel is at the maximum of 255 and the other ones at zero. And in green, basically the same happens for green. Next up we have white, and in white we have all the three colors at the maximum of 255.

So basically having all the colors at maximum gives us a complete white, while at the other end of the spectrum when we have all the colors at zero we get a complete black color. Finally, the other three colors that we have here are a mix of the other two colors that they are made of. So you see that this magenta here is red and blue at the maximum and no green at all. Then we have this, I think it's called cyan or cian color which has a red at zero and G and B at its maximum.

And finally, yellow has blue at zero and the other two at 255. Great. So I hope that this makes sense. And now that we have a very basic understanding of how the RGB model works, let's actually see how we can represent or how we can define colors in CSS. So in CSS, we have two ways of writing colors using the RGB model and those are the RGB notation and the hexadecimal notation. So by using the RGB notation, all we do is to use this RGB function in CSS.

And then we simply specify the values for each of the three color channels, red, green, and blue. So for example, if we set green and blue to the maximum values, then we get this cyan color just as we saw in the last slide. Another example, which is a lot more real world is this orange color right here. So here the numbers for each channel look a little bit more random. And so, this is how we get a real looking color using CSS and using the RGB notation.

Then besides the normal RGB function, there is also RGB with transparency, and transparency is also called alpha. And so that's why this function is called RGBA. So here we can specify a fourth value which in this case is the 0.3 and this will then give this color a transparency as we can see here. Looking at this other example if we for example, define an alpha value of 0.7, then we see that this color is actually transparent as visible when we put it on top of another color like this green square.

Now, of course, we don't have to manually come up with these numbers for these colors, okay? So we don't have to like manually write 244, 179, 63 in order to get this orange. So let's see, and indeed it worked. Now they are back to being bold. So we basically changed our selector here and added a pseudo-class to it. So both here and both here, because again, both of them are li elements that are now the last-child inside of its parent container.

Next up, we can actually also target a specific child. So for example, the third or the second child. So for that, we use the nth-child pseudo-class. And then here, we actually need to write parenthesis like this so we can specify which of the childs that we want. So let's say we want the second child to have a color of red. So you see number two, and here two and four, right? So this technique is quite useful, for example, to style tables, which oftentimes have like alternating background colors. Now finally, let me clear up a common misconception that there is around these pseudo-classes. So let's say that we wanted to select the first paragraph element that's inside of the article. So what I just said is basically article and then P. So that's the descendant selector, right?

So selecting a paragraph that's inside of the article, and now selecting the very first of that. So first-child. Now let's say we want the color to be red in this one. But as we reload this and check out our page, you see that nothing happened. So, no paragraph actually turned red. So again, the misconception is that this selector here should have selected the first P element inside of the article. And so this would be this one, right? So as we just saw before, this paragraph is, in fact, the first paragraph inside of the article.

However, this is not how the first-child pseudo-class actually works. Instead, what CSS will do is to select a P element that is actually the first-child of the article. All right? So the P element is the first P element inside of the article, but it is not the first-child of article. The first-child of article is actually header, right? It is not a paragraph. And so therefore this selector here does not work in the way that maybe we might think it would.

So this would only work if a paragraph would actually be the first element of the article. So let's do that. So if we save now, then indeed we get some red paragraph. So now this paragraph is the first-child of the article, and so therefore, now our selector applies. All right? Now let's see the end of our article. So it ends here and we can see that a paragraph is actually the last-child of the article element, right? And so what would work is this.

So let's see our result. And indeed now this text is red, and so it makes sense, right? Again, this worked because it is a P element inside of the article, and it is indeed the last-child of that article. And so therefore this selector then applied, and did exactly what it should do. So basically what this means is that when we mix multiple elements inside of a parent element, then these pseudo-classes don't work really well. They are however perfect for situations like this one where all the child elements are the same.

So in a list like ul or ol, all the child elements are supposed to be li. And so, then this pseudo-class, like first-child, last-child, or nth-child work perfectly. Well, let's learn what rules CSS applies in order to resolve conflicting declarations like this one. So when there are multiple declarations for the exact same element, such as we have here in our example, then what matters are the selectors. So the highest priority for now are the ID selectors. So that means if there is any ID selector, then that is the rule that is going to be applied. Now, if there are multiple ID selectors, then it is the last of those selectors that gets applied.

Now, in reality, it is actually a bit more complicated than this. So there are a lot of concepts involved, such as the cascade and selector specificity, but you don't need to know about these details for now as a beginner. So I think that the amount of information that I will give you in this slide should be enough for you to resolve your own conflicts in your own CSS code. All right. But anyway, in case there is no ID selector, then the next in the priority is a class or a pseudo-class selector.

And again, if there are multiple of one of those, then it is the last selector of those in the code that gets applied. Then the next is the element selector. So in case there is no ID selector or no class selector, then it is the element selector that gets applied. And again, if there are multiple, it is the last one of those. Finally, there's also something called the universal selector, but a bit more about that in the next lecture. What matters is that the universal selector is the one with the lowest priority of all, alright?

But now, going back to our example and taking into consideration the rules that we have here, we should now be able to resolve the conflict that we have here. So we have a class selector, then we have an ID selector, and then we have an element selector, right? So based on the rules that we just learned here, it is the ID selector with the idea of author text that will decide the font size of this element. So for the conflicting font size property, it is this ID selector that actually gets applied.

But keep in mind that the font style, font family, and the color from all the other selectors still applies, right? So that's what I mentioned in the last slide. So if we have multiple rules, so multiple selectors that select the same element, then all of those rules apply. All right. And these are the most important rules that you need to know to resolve conflicting declarations. Then with the highest priority, we have declarations marked with the important keywords. And the important keywords is basically just a hack that you can use as the last resort to resolve conflicts in your CSS. But this should usually not be used. And so basically what this means is that inheritance is a mechanism by which some styles, so some properties get their values inherited from parent elements to child elements.

And so, let's now use this in a big way by setting some styles onto the body element. So we use the body elements to set some styles because the body element is the parent element of all the other elements in our HTML document. And so, if we set certain properties in the body, then their values will get inherited to all of their child elements. Now, not all properties do actually get inherited, it is mostly the ones that are about text. So let's start with a very simple one.

Well, let's see. And so as we reload, nothing really changed here. And the reason for that is that while this red color still got inherited, this colored property right here in this rule did override the inherited style, okay. So the inherited styles are easily overwritten whenever there is any rule that applies for the same property.

So an inherited property is very easily overwritten by any rule which has a value for that same property. So in a sense, we can say that inherited values are the ones who have the lowest priority. But anyway, if we now removed the color from here, and let's just comment it out, then well, all the text which does not have a color declared will become red. LECTURE 3.14: CSS Theory #3: The CSS Box Model
----------------------------------------

Jonas: The CSS box model is one of the most fundamental parts of CSS, and so you really need to understand it in order to learn CSS. And so that is exactly what we will do in this video. Now, what exactly is the box model? Well, the box model defines how elements are displayed on a webpage and how they are sized. So in this box model, each and every element on a webpage can be seen as a rectangular box, and each of these boxes can have content, a border, and space inside and outside of it.

So let's define all of the pieces of the box model one by one. And starting with the content, this is the actual content of the element. So it can be text or images, or a table, a video, or really any other content that we might specify. Using CSS properties, we can specify both the height and the width of the content area which we will do in one of the next lectures. Next, we can define a border that goes all around the element. And actually we already did that before, remember?

And by the way, this border is technically still inside of the element. And now the next ingredient of the box model is the padding. So padding is basically invisible white space that we can create around the elements content. So between the content and the border. You can see that nicely in this diagram and it will make even more sense when we start using this in practice. But anyway, just like the border, the padding is also still inside of the element.

So essentially, padding is empty space that we can create inside of elements. Then similar to padding, we also have margin. Now the difference is that margin creates empty space around the element, so outside of the element itself. So in practice, we use margin in order to create space between elements on our page. So if for example, we want space between two certain elements, we simply specify the margin property on one of them. So again, padding is empty space that we can add inside of any element.

It will sit between the content itself and the border which is basically the outermost part of the element. So the content, padding, and border altogether are the visible part of the element as we can see it on the page. Then around all that, we can add some margin in order to create space between elements. Now, what's important to note here is that all of these are actually optional, so we don't have to specify paddings or a border or margins. So we can define none of them or some, or even all of them.

It all depends on how we want our layout to look like. Finally, there is also something called the fill area. And this one can be a bit confusing, but let's try to understand it. So remember that the text content and images are inside the content box, right? Now, the same does not apply for background images or the background color of an element. These properties will actually be applied not only to the content area, but to the entire fill area, which also includes the padding and the border.

So basically if we apply a background image or color, it'll occupy the entire visible part of the element. Now, for some people, this can all sound very abstract and hard to imagine in the real world. And so in these situations, it's very useful to think of an analogy in the real world. And one analogy that I personally find very helpful is to imagine a frame on a wall. So in this analogy, the drawing or the image that is in the frame is the content area.

Then, many frames actually have this like kind of white paper between the drawing or the image and the actual frame itself. And so if we bring that back to our box model, then that would of course be the padding. So the space between the content area and the border. And so in this analogy, the frame is of course the border, right? So that makes a lot of sense. Finally, when we hang a picture on the wall using a frame like this, then of course there might be some space between other elements on the wall or even some other walls on the sides.

And so in our box model analogy, that of course would be the margin. So it is the space that is outside of the frame and creating space between frames. So for example, there might be another frame somewhere here on the wall, and the space between those frames, so outside of them, is what we call the margin in the box model. Okay? So hopefully this analogy from the real world helps you bring these concepts back into the more abstract world of CSS.

And now just to finish, let's quickly learn how the box model actually calculates the exact size of an element based on content, border, and padding. So as I mentioned, we can specify the height and the width of the content area. Now, if we choose not to define the height or width, then the box model will simply imply them based on the content. However, the specified or implied heights and width are actually not the final sizes of the element and that's because the border and the padding are also taken into account.

So the final width of an element, as we see it in the final layout, is defined by the left border plus the left padding plus the specified or implied width plus the right padding plus the right border. And the same logic of course applies to the height of an element. So it's the top border plus the top padding plus the specified or implied height plus the bottom padding, and finally, the bottom border. Now, as you can see, the margin is of course not part of the width or height calculations of the elements because again, it is just space that is around them.

And as I said in the beginning of the lecture, we can of course specify all these individual sizes using certain CSS properties. Now, what's very important to note here is that this way of calculating heights and width is actually just the default behavior of the box model. However, we can change this default behavior because it actually doesn't make much sense and we will do that a bit later. But for now, I don't want to confuse you anymore. And so let's start by using this default behavior starting right in the next video.

LECTURE 3.17: Centering our Page

-: One of the very first tricks that I learned with CSS was how to center a page inside of the browser. So back in the day, many pages were not centered, and I found it really cool that we could very easily center a page in the browser using a very simple trick. And so let me now share that really nice trick with you in this video. Now, the very first thing that we need to do in order to pull off this trick is to put all of our content into a container element, because otherwise if we don't do that, then what is there actually to center in the window?

So what I mean is that right now as we keep resizing the browser window all of the content actually stretches from one side to the other. So there is no content there to center in the center of the browser, right? So we first need a container, and that container then needs a certain width. So let's put all of this into a box. And this box doesn't need to have any special meaning. So we don't need a semantic html element here. And so we can simply use a div element.

Now this one should not close here, but it should close right before the end of the body. So it starts right there and we close it only here after the footer. And now as I save it, all the indentation should automatically get fixed, and it did. Nice. So this is a really nice thing about Prettier. So when we keep adding other elements then all the annotation will automatically get fixed which is really, really helpful. Then here we need to give this a name and I like to use the name of "container".

Let's copy that class, and style it here. And as I was saying now we actually need to give this container a width because otherwise there is not really anything to center. So let's start with 700 pixels, and I'll make it a bit wider later. Okay, so we have this width of 700 pixels now. So you see that now the width of this element so this header here, which is a child element of the container, is now only 700 to pixels as well. So again, this div here has a width of 700, so we can see that here.

And so now the child elements which are inside of it can of course not be bigger than that. So they can only be as large as the container element. And so therefore this one is also 600px wide or actually 700. So that 620 plus 40 plus 40, okay? So this has nothing to do, like, with inheritance or something like that. Instead, it is simply the logic that the child element can never be wider than the parent element. And so if the parent element is 700 then all the others are going to be 700 as well.

So this one for example is 700 and the H2 as well and so on and so forth. Right. The same here goes for the image of course which is 100% of the parent. And so now as we keep making this bigger these 700 pixel container here always keep staying on the left side. And so now as a final step we need to center this container element inside of the browser. And so that is the actual trick. So giving the container a width is part one. And now part two is to add some margins to the left and to the right of the container.

So we can say margin left and then set it to auto, which stands for automatic. And margin to the right also automatic. So what this means is that the margin on the left needs to be the same, then the margin on the right side and they should both be calculated automatically by the browser. And so therefore this will mean that there will be a margin on the left and on the right which will be exactly the same size, and therefore as a result the container will look centered inside of the body.

So basically inside of the browser. So if we give this a save, then it does actually work. Great. This is fantastic. So as we resize, let's see then the margin on the left and on the right keep growing and they keep giving us basically this illusion that the page is completely centered so that the container is centered. So if I inspect this now and go to the container then here I can see that the margin is right now 180 on both sides. And if I resize this then you see that now it is only for example 72.5 on each side.

So again, it is the same on both sides because it is auto on both sides. And auto means that the browser will automatically figure out the width. Okay. Now here actually I want this to be 800 pixels, but I put it a bit smaller before because if we then put it like this we can actually not not see anything. So it doesn't look centered. LECTURE 3.20: CSS Theory #5: Absolute Positioning

-: Let's talk about another extremely important aspect of CSS, which are positioning modes. And this one, is one of the more complex lectures of this section. And so make sure to pay good attention. So in CSS there are a couple of different positioning modes, but the more important ones and the ones we are gonna talk about for now are the normal flow and absolute positioning. So starting with normal flow, it is simply the default positioning of elements on our page.

Or we can also achieve the normal flow by setting position to the value of relative. So in this case we say that an element is in flow, which basically means that the elements are laid out according to the source code in the html. So this is very straightforward. It is simply the behavior that we have been seeing up until this point. So just keep in mind that that is called normal flow. Now on the other hand, we have absolute positioning, which basically allows us to absolutely position elements anywhere on the page.

Now we can achieve this positioning mode. So we can position an element absolutely by setting its position property to the value of absolute. And so in this case, the element is then removed from the normal flow and we say that it is out of flow. Now what happens with this element is that it completely loses any impact on surrounding elements and in fact it might even overlap them. So that's something common that happens with absolutely positioned elements.

Now, in order to actually position the element that is absolutely positioned, we can use the top, bottom, left, or right properties in order to position that element and that positioning is going to happen in relation to a relatively positioned container. Now I know that this sounds kind of confusing and so let's actually see this happening in practice. And so therefore, it will be located exactly 100 pixels from the top of its relatively positioned container element and 200 pixels from the left of its again, first relatively positioned container element. And it's important to mention that it is the first parent element that has positioned set to relative from which the absolutely positioned element will be placed. LECTURE 4.2: The 3 Ways of Building Layouts
----------------------------------------

Instructor: This entire section is all about building layouts. And so, before we actually start doing that, let's talk about what layout actually means and also the three major ways in which we can build layouts in CSS right now. So, in web design and web development, when we say layout, what we mean is basically the way that text, images, and all the other content is placed and arranged on the webpage. So here on the right side I have an example of a very simple website and there are a couple of pieces of content.

And clearly, they are arranged in a certain way, right? And so, again, the way in which they are arranged and placed here on this website is the layout of the design essentially. So the layout gives this page what we call a visual structure, and then into that structure we can place the content. Now, one of the main jobs as front end developers, so as HTML, CSS, and JavaScript developers, is to build layouts which is the reason why we have an entire section on building layouts alone.

So, according to this definition of layout, building a layout means to arrange page elements into some kind of visual structure instead of simply having all of our elements, so all of our content, basically placed one after another. Just imagine that in this example website all these seven pieces of content would simply be laid out one after the other. That wouldn't look very interesting visually, right? And it also would it make a lot harder to actually understand the content that is being transmitted here.

So, layout exists for a reason because it makes our sites easier to understand and also makes it visually more pleasing. Now, there are basically two types of layouts which are page layout and component layout. So page layout is basically what I've been talking about up until this point, which is laying out the elements. So the big pieces of content inside of a webpage or a website. Now, on the other hand, these bigger page layouts are themselves made up of components like this one.

And these components themselves need to have some kind of layout because these components themselves are made out of smaller pieces of content, which also need to be arranged in some kind of way. And so we can say that components themselves also have a layout. So once again, we wouldn't want to have these 12 pieces of content simply laid out one after another, right? That wouldn't make a lot of sense. And so therefore, we also need to give the smaller components some kind of layout.

Okay, so now that we know what layouts are and what type of layouts we can build, now let's see how we can actually build them with CSS. And the first technique of building layouts in CSS is using float layouts, which is basically the old way of building layouts using the float CSS property. Now, these types of layouts are quickly getting replaced by newer technologies such as Flexbox and CSS Grid, but in some cases they are still being used and especially on older websites.

So we will still learn how to build float layouts just so you know how they work in case you ever see one at some point in your career. For example, when you're working on a older website. But for the main part, we will then quickly move on to one of the newer ways of building layouts which is using Flexbox. So Flexbox is one of the modern ways of laying out elements. And in the case of Flexbox, it is perfect for building one dimensional layouts.

So basically a layout which is just a row and all without using floats. So Flexbox might be perfect for simpler component layouts just like we saw in the last slide. Then the other modern way of laying out elements is CSS Grid. So with CSS Grid we can actually build complete two dimensional layouts which is perfect for big page layouts and also more complex components like the one that we saw in the last slide. So Flexbox and CSS Grid have completely revolutionized the way in which we build layouts in CSS right now.

And so we will spend most of the course learning them and using them in our big website project later. But for now, let's actually start quickly learning float layouts in the next lecture.

It is instead nav. Okay? And now it's more on the right side and if we open up... Well, actually, it doesn't change anything for now. But what matters is that this here is now floated to the right side and this one to the left side. Now, the interesting thing that's happening and that I wanted to show you is if you notice this gray background here, and maybe we can make it a bit more obvious, so this header, let's change this here quickly to red, and so now what we can see here is that this element kind of lost its height.

So it looks very weird. In fact, the only reason why it is still visible is because we have some padding here. So if we remove the padding, then this element would disappear completely. So at least the background color behind it. So why is this happening? Well, the reason is that all of its child elements, which are in this case only two, right? So the header only has two child elements: the h1 and the nav, and right now, all of them are floated.

This means that it's as if these elements would not even be on the page. So as if they had been removed. And so now the element basically has no content anymore. And so that way it makes sense that its height is actually zero. So again, the height is now as if it was zero. The only remaining space that is remaining is because of the padding, and if we come down here to the box model, we can see that. So the width is still 720 but the height is in indeed zero.

And it's only this padding of 20 pixels on both sides that is still making this element visible. But otherwise, the background color would completely disappear. So exactly what happens if we put this here, the first one to zero. Right? So this phenomena is what we call the collapsing element and when this happens, we say that the element's height has collapsed. And again, this did happen because both of its children are now floated. So it's as if they were not on the page anymore.

Now, of course, we do not want that, right? So we still want this element here to have the height that it had before. We can actually fix that, which is exactly what we will do in the next lecture. But for now, just to finish, let's quickly review how floats work and compare them to absolute positioning. Now, floats are actually not a positioning scheme like absolute positioning but they are still another way in which elements can be out of flow.

And so it actually makes sense to compare it with absolute positioning. So we can achieve a floating element by using float: left or float: right just as we we learned before. And as I was just saying, when an element is floated, it is removed out of the normal flow. And so in this regard, it is exactly the same as with absolute positioning. Now, what's different about floats is that floated elements do still have an impact on surrounding elements.

So text and inline elements will actually wrap around the floated element. And so again, in this regard, floated elements are completely different from absolutely positioned elements, which have no impact and are also not impacted by any of the surrounding elements. Finally, one important characteristic of floats is that the container element will simply not adjust its height to the floated element. And so this is exactly the reason why in the last example that we just saw, we saw that that container element collapsed its height.

Now right, so I hope this quick overview and comparison will make it easier for you to understand floats and so in the next lecture, as I was saying, we will now fix that problem of collapsing heights. So see you there soon.

However, clearing floats like this only really works on a block level element. And so we set the display property on this element to "block". And so with this, the problem should now be fixed as well. And indeed, there you go. So, let's check that out quickly. And so here is that pseudo element that we just created. And just to remember, this is the default way of the box model calculating the elements width and the heights. So as we've seen in practice many times, whenever we specify a height or a width, then the box model will add the border and the padding on top of that.

So that's a nice and simple trick that actually every single CSS developer uses. So it would be completely impossible to build large layouts without using box sizing board or box. So again, the default way of the box model actually doesn't make any sense at all. So instead, everyone simply adds box sizing border box to all elements, which will then forever fix the kind of problems that we just experienced. So as we can see in this new diagram where box sizing has been set to border box, now the specified width and height goes all the way from one side of the border to the opposite side of the border, including of course the content area and the padding.

And so now, the final width and height calculations are very simple. There's actually nothing left to calculate. So the final width of any element will simply be exactly the width that we define in our code no matter the padding and borders. And the same of course goes for the height. So if we now define some paddings or borders they will not get added to the dimensions of the box which really makes our lives so much easier. Now, what this also means at the same time is that padding and borders that we do specify will now reduce the inner width of the content area, but that's usually not a problem.

LECTURE 4.9: A Flexbox Overview
----------------------------------------

-: Let's now define what exactly Flexbox is and when and why we need it, and also talk about some important terminology around Flexbox. And finally also get an overview of all the properties that are part of the Flexbox specification. So a one line definition of Flexbox is that it is a set of related CSS properties that we can use to build one dimensional layouts. Now, when Flex Box was developed a couple of years ago, the main idea behind it was to basically allow browsers to automatically divide empty space inside some container element, by its child elements.

And by doing that, the browser takes away a lot of work that previously the web developers had to do so by defining manually with and stuff like that. So a bit like we did in our last coding challenge. So with Flex Box, all of that would happen automatically. Now, Flex Box also makes it extremely easy to automatically align items to one another inside a certain parent container. And that is true both horizontally and vertically. And in fact, we already saw that working a little bit in the previous lecture, right?

And so with this Flexbox solves a couple of very common problems in CSS development such as vertical centering and also creating equal height columns. So these used to be hard problems before Flex Box came along. But now with modern css, these are very, very simple to solve. And so since you are learning CSS only now with these modern technologies already in place you will never know how difficult this used to be. So consider yourself very lucky by that.

So basically what I just said is that Flex Box is perfect for replacing the old school floats, and by that it allows us to write fewer and also cleaner HTML NCSS codes which of course is very easy to maintain websites over the long run and to write less bucks. Okay, so now that we know what Flex Box is exactly and what problems it helps us solve, let's talk a little bit about some important terminology. And actually there are not many concepts behind Flexbox that you need to understand in order to start using it.

But here is what you do need to know. So first of all, the element on which we want to use Flexbox is called the Flex container. So just as I mentioned in the last lecture as well. And all we have to do in order to create a flex container is to set its display property to flex, and that's it. That's how we get started with Flexbox. So if we do this, then all the direct children of that flex container will become the so-called flex items. And this is actually important to know and to keep in mind because we will use different properties on the flex container and on the flex items.

Now, the direction in which these flex items are laid out is called the main axis. Which is represented with this arrow here. Then the other perpendicular axis is simply called the cross axis, and it's important to know about these names because we can actually change the direction of the main access, and so therefore also of the cross axis. Plus we can align elements along the main axis and along the cross axis in different ways. And therefore we always need to know which axis we are dealing with.

So try to keep these concepts in mind so that you can fully understand how the different Flexbox related properties work. And actually that's what we're gonna talk about next. So in this slide, before we actually move to the practice part. I want to show you an overview of all the CSS properties that are part of the Flexbox specification, both for the flex container and for the flex items. So for the flex container the most important ones are the gap, the justify content, and the aligned items properties.

And in fact, we already talked about two of them in the last lecture, right? Now, I'm not going to go over all the details here. Just know that the first value that is in bold is the default value. And then the other ones are the possible options that we can specify. And then also you have a very short description of each of the properties. And so my hope is that you can use this slide kind of as a cheat sheet to print out or to create a print screen image that you can always have handy when you are working with Flexbox.

I actually did this in the very beginning when I started learning Flexbox, and it was really, really helpful because it is in fact impossible to know all of these properties by heart at all times and also know exactly what they do. So again, I think it would be a great idea to print out the slide and keep it as a cheat sheet close to your keyboard or whatever you use on your working space. But anyway, there are 3 other properties that we can apply on the flex container element which are flex direction, flex wrap, and aligned content.

And actually, some of these, especially number 5 and 6, are used for pretty advanced Flexbox techniques that we will not study in this course because I think they are a bit too confusing for beginners. So in this course, which is more of a beginner CSS course my goal is just that you really understand the fundamentals of Flexbox and are able to use them on your own. And with these fundamentals, trust me you can solve 99% of all the most common scenarios.

But now moving on a bit to properties that we can apply on the flex items themselves. One of them is Align auto which is pretty important because this can basically override the aligned items property. Then we have these other ones, which are flex grow flex shrink, flex bases, and D 3 together. So 2, 3, and 4 form the flex property. So as you can see below number 5 there Flex is the recommended shorthand for flex grow, flex shrink and flex bases.

Okay? And again, we will go over them a little bit later in the section once we actually can start using them in practice. Finally, there is also the order property which we can use to basically change the order of the flex items visually on the page without changing their order in the source code. Okay, but enough talking now, let's now move back to code and start learning many of these properties 1 by 1.

LECTURE 4.16: A CSS Grid Overview
----------------------------------------

-: Now that you know some of the fundamentals of CSS Grid in practice, let's now also learn some theory about it. And so just like with Flex Books, the first question that we ask is what actually is CSS Grid? And at the most basic level, CSS Grid is a set of CSS properties that web developers can use to build 2-dimensional layouts. And when CSS Grid was first developed and brought into browsers a couple of years ago, the main idea behind it was that now we could divide a container element into rows and columns that we could then fill with it's child elements.

And a lot of stuff is possible here. So things like spending elements across multiple rows and columns overlap different elements and more. So we use CSS Grid in 2-dimensional contexts where it allows us to write a lot less than HTML and also easier to read CSS. And you will start appreciating these characteristics of CSS Grid once you actually start using it and maybe comparing it to things like Flex Books or even float layouts. So CSS Grid completely changes the way that we envision and build 2-dimensional layouts with CSS.

And therefore we can say that in a way, CSS Grid completely revolutionized CSS. Now one common misconception that many beginners have is that CSS Grid is meant to replace Flex Books. However that is really not the case. So, instead Flex Books and CSS Grid work together perfectly. You simply use them in different situations. So when you need a 1-dimensional layout, then you can simply reach for flex books. But if you meed a 2-dimensional layout, which is usually a grid anyway, then you can use CSS Grid for that.

So again, one does not replace the other but instead they work together really nicely. And now we need to, once again, talk about some terminology here so that when I talk about CSS Grid we are all on the same page here. So as we just learned, already actually, the grid container is basically where everything happens and we create a grid container by setting it's display property to grid. Then all the child elements of the grid container will be the grid items.

So again, just like we learned before, and also this is quite similar to Flex Books. Right? Then, also like Flex Books, we also have axis here. So we have a row axis, and a column axis. Now unlike Flex Books, we cannot change the direction of the row and column axis. Which in my opinion actually makes it even a bit easier to work with CSS Grid. All right, so this is the basic terminology about CSS Grid. However, since 2-dimensional layouts are a bit more complex, we need actually some more terminology in order to really understand what's going on.

So let's look at some more terminology here. So this is what we just saw before, but now lets also introduce the concept of grid lines which are these lines which basically divide up the grids and separate the columns and the rows. And as you can see, these grid lines are numbered from 1 to the number of columns plus 1. And the number of rows plus 1. So if we have 3 columns, then we have 4 grid lines for the columns. And if we have 2 rows then we have 3 grid lines for the rows.

And these numbers are actually important because we can use them to place a grid item exactly in one place in the grid where we want it to be. Now the intersection of all these grid lines, so both the grid lines for the columns and the rows, and creates all these areas in which we can place, or grid, items. And these areas are called the grid cells. Okay. So grid cells are always created but they don't always need to be filled. So in this case, we only have 5 grid items but there are still 6 cells.

Simply because this is a grid with 3 columns and 2 rows. And so 3x2 makes 6. So, again, each of these spaces is called a grid cell. But they don't always need to be filled by a grid item. And also, they don't need to be filled entirely. Next up, as we saw in the last lecture we can actually create spaces between the grid items. And these are then called gutters or gaps. So, remember, for that we use the gap property or also the row gap and column gap property.

So technically these are actually called gutters. Okay? Finally, another term that is commonly used when we talk about CSS Grid is the term of grid track. So, a grid track can be a row or also a column. So each of these are grid tracks and so in this example here we have 2 row tracks and 3 column tracks. Okay? And we call these tracks because these concepts are a bit more about the space itself and not about the grid items. So, a little bit like a grid cell.

Right? So remember a grid cell might be filled by a grid item or not. But what matters is there is some theoretical space. And the same applies to the grid track. Okay, but now I promise that's it about terminology. And I know that this is a lot to take in, so please don't worry too much about all these terms at this point. So with time, this will come naturally to you. Especially things like grid cell, the grid lines, and the gutters or gaps. So these are important terms that we are going to use all the time.

And so at some point, you will naturally know about these. And now, to finish, just like in the Flex Books lecture, let's now take a look at an overview of some of the properties that we can use on the grid container and on the grid item. And starting with the properties for the grid container, the most important ones are the grid-template-rows, grid template columns, the column-gap, and row-gap; which together make up the gap property. And then also justify-items and align-items which we can use to align the items inside rows, or inside columns.

So in other words, horizontally and vertically. So just like before I have to default value for each of the properties and a short description. So I think it would be very helpful for you if you could print out this overview, kind of like a cheat sheet, so you can have it handy whenever you start writing your own CSS Grid code. So I will not go over all of these here now one-by-one because of course we will do that in practice. But anyway, there's also two less important properties on the grid container which are justified-content and align-content.

So these only apply if the container is actually larger than the grid. And so these are usually not that important. And right away, actually this overview of the CSS Grid properties does not contain all of them. So there is actually a huge amount of CSS grid properties, but we will not talk about all of them here in this course. Because that would be just too confusing for beginners. This course should be comfortable for you as a CSS beginner and therefore we are not going to over complicate things to much.

All right, so anyway, now about the grid items. There is the grid-column and the grid-row properties, which are very important to place grid items into a specific cell. Then finally we have justify-self and align-self, which hopefully you can recognize from Flex Books. So align-self is used to override align items and justify-self is used to override justified items for one individual grid cell. So, again, just like in Flex Books. So, this is an overview of the most important CSS Grid properties that we are gonna use in this course.

So make sure to print this out and have it next to your keyboard once we start writing codes in the next lecture.

LECTURE 5.3: Overview of Web Design and Website Personalities
----------------------------------------

Instructor: Now, before we can learn about the different web design rules one by one we need to start by talking about what web design actually is, why it's so important, and also why and how everyone can learn good web design. So first of all, we need to distinguish between web design and web development. So basically, web designers are who create the overall look and feel of websites. While on the other hand, web developers are the ones who then implement the design using html CSS and JavaScript code.

Now, back in the day, designers only designed using some web design program such as Sketch, Figma or Photoshop. The developer would then take that design and implement it in code using some software such as VS code so that in the end, the website could be displayed for the user in a browser. However, nowadays, there are also many designers who code and many developers who design. And so the goal of this section is to transform you to a developer who also designs so that basically, you can become a designer and a developer who can write and build and design websites only using code.

So our focus in this course will of course be learning HTML and CSS, so basically writing code. But in my opinion, a modern web developer should also be able to create simple and good-looking designs. And so that's what I want to teach you in this section. But first, let's explore a little bit why design is actually so important. So when a user visits a well-designed website or web application, then that good design immediately creates a lasting good impression of the brand or the product that is behind that website.

However, if the site was badly designed, then the user would believe that the brand doesn't really care about the product or the service that they're offering. And so, when you build a website, of course, you do not want to create that impression, right? Also, good design makes the user trust the brand right away. While on the other hand, a website with bad design makes the user insecure about even trusting that company or the brand. Another really important reason for investing a lot of time and effort into a well-designed product is that good design increases the perceived value of the brand or the product that the user is visiting.

While bad design simply makes the brand look kind of cheap, and I'm sure that you have experienced this yourself when you for example, check out two competing websites of two competing products. So probably you get a better impression of the product that has the good-looking website and you also trust the brand more and kind of feel that that product is worth more, at least for me, it sure works like this, and there's a lot of research indicating that this is how it works for the general users.

And so again, it's really, really important that you or your company or whoever you're working for invest in really good design for their websites and web applications. Finally, good design also gives users exactly what they were actually looking for when they decided to come to the site in the first place. For example, let's say you are looking to buy a TV. So in that case, you want that webpage for the TV to give you all the information as fast as possible.

And so for that, it's important that the page is well designed. You don't want to be confused and have to leave the page because you cannot reach your goal, right? And that's what would happen if the page was badly designed. Now, okay, and I hope that with this, I could convince you that design cannot just be an afterthought. It needs to be central to building any product. So any website or any web application. Now, many people are already aware about how important web design is, however, they will say something like, oh, I'm not creative, or, well, I'm not an artist and so I could never learn design.

However, in my opinion, that is not really true because good web design is actually not subjective and has not much to do with creativity. For example, I myself couldn't be any further from being an artist, and I'm also not particularly creative, but still, I can design a decent-looking interface by following a simple framework or a system such as the one that I want to teach you in this course. And so, I really believe that anyone can learn good web design.

You don't need to be creative, and you don't need to be an artist. All you need to do is to learn some rules and some guidelines along with some system that you then need to follow in order to build a nice-looking interface for your own projects. Now, what kind of framework or system will I actually teach you, and how am I gonna do that? Well, what I did was to analyze hundreds or maybe thousands of really well-designed websites. So I carefully analyzed and deconstructed the design of all these websites and then distilled everything that I learned into a couple of rules that are easy for you to learn, and even more importantly, easy to apply.

Now, these rules are divided into nine different areas of web design, which I call the ingredients, and you will see what the ingredients are in a minute. But what matters is that there are many different rules for each of these ingredients.
